source: Li et al. (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: hierarchical legal reasoning (CATO-based)
finding: Six LLMs were tested on CATO-style factor-hierarchy reasoning between a current case and a precedent. Surface distinctions were solved by all. Hierarchical roles were harder. Integrated 'significant distinction' analysis collapsed.
numbers: 253 case pairs per task, each case 4 factors. Task 1: 100% all models. Task 2: 64.82% (gemini-2.5-flash) to 92.09% (gpt-5). Task 3: 11.46% (gemini-flash) to 33.99% (qwen3-thinking); most under 25%.
quote: models achieve high accuracy on surface-level distinctions
limits: Synthetic pairs from the CATO trade-secret factor set only; one domain; temperature 0.3.
agent_relevance: The HYPO/CATO distinguish step is easy alone but fails when steps must be chained. Our map-an-analogue operator should split into separate checked sub-steps, not one prompt.

source: Li et al. (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: hierarchical legal reasoning (CATO-based) - thinking vs non-thinking
finding: Reasoning-trained models beat the same model without thinking on factor-hierarchy tasks.
numbers: qwen3-235b: thinking 78.66% vs non-thinking 30.04% on Task 2 (2.6x); Task 3: 33.99% vs 0.00%.
limits: One model family; confound of RL post-training versus token count.
agent_relevance: Explicit deliberation is needed for case comparison; a plain one-shot analogy call is unsafe.

source: Li et al. (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: hierarchical legal reasoning (CATO-based) - token cost
finding: More thinking tokens did not mean better answers. Wrong answers used more tokens than right ones.
numbers: Task 2 thinking tokens: gpt-5 3,189 for 92.09% vs gemini-pro 5,144 for 64.82% vs qwen3-thinking 9,596 for 78.66% (table rows partly misaligned in extraction; text confirms gpt-5 3,189 and qwen3-thinking 9,596). gpt-5 incorrect Task 2 answers 4,456 tokens vs 3,081 correct (+45%). Task 3 up to about 15,678 tokens.
limits: Token counts depend on vendor reporting.
agent_relevance: Use a long analogy trace as a warning sign of a stuck mapping; cut and re-plan.

source: Li et al. (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: hierarchical legal reasoning (CATO-based) - structure given as input
finding: The CATO hierarchy was supplied as a Mermaid diagram in the prompt, with rule definitions of distinction types (emphasizing, downplaying).
numbers: Prompt templates in Appendix C; 5 reasoning LLMs plus 1 non-reasoning.
limits: No ablation of the diagram format is reported.
agent_relevance: Giving the structure of relevance (what counts as a similarity) in the prompt is the HYPO/CATO way of scaffolding an analogy.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal Question Answering
finding: Used the CBR retrieve step to feed past legal cases into the LLM prompt. Compared BERT, LegalBERT and AnglEBERT embeddings with inter, intra and hybrid similarity.
numbers: Case base from Australian Open Legal QA (57% of cases had no reference to legal acts). Best: hybrid AnglEBERT weights [0.25,0.40,0.35], k=3 full cases, cosine 0.9141, about +1.94% over No-RAG. Significant vs No-RAG and hybrid LegalBERT k=3 at 95% (one-tailed t-test); only 90% vs hybrid BERT k=1.
limits: Gain is small; No-RAG baseline already high since the model has parametric memory; metric is semantic similarity to a reference answer, not legal correctness; only retrieve and reuse, no revise or retain.
agent_relevance: Case retrieval helps a little on a strong base model. Do not expect large gains from naive precedent lookup. Indexing by several fields beat one field.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal Question Answering - full case vs support only
finding: Putting the full case in the prompt gave better answers than only the support text in most hybrid variants. LegalBERT, though trained on legal text, did worse than AnglEBERT.
numbers: Cosine scores 0.89-0.91 across k=1 and k=3 (Table 4).
limits: Small differences; single dataset.
agent_relevance: Store cases whole (problem, solution, reasoning) in memory, not just a summary line.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: A planner-executor LLM agent with a case bank (state, action, reward) and CBR retrieval, no weight updates. Cites Ashley (1992) for case-based reasoning.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3 (top-1 when published), test 79.40%. DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM. SimpleQA 95.0%. Case memory adds 4.7 to 9.6 absolute points on out-of-distribution tasks. Planner GPT-4.1, executor o3 (GAIA) or o4-mini.
limits: Leaderboard comparison with different base models; memory holds task trajectories, not legal precedents; validation cases seeded the test case bank.
agent_relevance: Direct example of CBR inside an agent loop: retrieve, reuse, revise (write back outcome), retain. Matches our subgoal memory.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs - number of retrieved cases
finding: Few cases are best. Accuracy peaks near K=4 then flattens or slightly drops.
numbers: DeepResearcher avg: K=0 59.9 F1 / 72.2 PM; K=1 63.6/77.9; K=4 64.5/78.5 (best); K=8 64.1/78.2; K=32 63.9/78.1. First case gives most of the gain (+3.7 F1).
limits: One benchmark set; authors note larger K adds noise and cost.
agent_relevance: Retrieve about 1 to 4 cases, not dozens.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs - learning curve
finding: Accumulated cases improved accuracy over five passes; learned (parametric) retrieval beat plain similarity retrieval, which beat no CBR.
numbers: Iter1 to Iter5 on DeepResearcher: no CBR 78.65 to 84.47; non-parametric CBR 79.84 to 84.85; parametric CBR 80.46 to 85.44. Gap to no-CBR shrinks from 1.8 to about 1.0 points.
limits: Gap is small and narrowing; no variance reported.
agent_relevance: Utility-weighted case retrieval gives a small edge over similarity alone, like CATO's weighing of case relevance.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI)
finding: Agent stores successful trajectories (retrieved as in-context cases) and also distils rules from success and failure pairs using ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE operators. A case plus rule hybrid like legal CBR.
numbers: Ablation insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%. Reflexion table: ReAct+Reflexion 40.3% at R0 to 54.4% at R3; ExpeL 59.0% to 64.2% (rows partly garbled in extracted text, read by order).
limits: Table layout garbled in extraction; GPT-3.5/4 era models; ALFWorld and HotpotQA only.
agent_relevance: Cases or rules: which is better depends on the task. Open QA gained from rules, action tasks from cases. Keep both, as legal CBR does.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI) - retrieval criterion
finding: Retrieving by task similarity gave the best examples; reasoning-similarity and random retrieval did worse.
numbers: ALFWorld ablation: values 48.5 and 42.5 for the two alternates versus 59.0 for task-similarity ExpeL (labels by order; text says task similarity wins).
limits: Garbled table; one environment.
agent_relevance: Similarity must be defined by what matters, as HYPO's dimensions do. Poor similarity is near random.

source: Magesh et al. (2024) Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools
finding: Preregistered test of commercial legal RAG tools. RAG reduces but does not remove fabrication of cases and holdings.
numbers: Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research and Ask Practical Law AI hallucinate 17% to 33% of the time. Lexis+ AI accurate on 65% of queries; Westlaw AI-AR accurate 42% and hallucinates nearly twice as often as other legal tools; Practical Law incomplete on over 60%. GPT-4 compared.
quote: each hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time
limits: Closed vendor systems; queries built by authors; 2024 snapshot.
agent_relevance: Retrieved cases can be wrongly characterised or overruled (Casey example). A retrieval step needs a validity check before reuse.

source: Dahl et al. (2024) Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in LLMs
finding: General LLMs often invent facts about real federal cases. Worse at lower courts and on older, less cited cases.
numbers: Hallucination 58% (ChatGPT 4) to 88% (Llama 2) on direct case questions; ChatGPT 3.5 69%, PaLM 2 72%. Doctrinal agreement task (do two cases agree, from Shepard's codes) near 0.5 hallucination, little better than chance.
quote: LLMs hallucinate at least 58% of the time
limits: 2023 models; questions on case facts, not full arguments; federal courts only.
agent_relevance: Analogical judgement between two cases was near chance without retrieval. Ground the analogue in retrieved text.

source: Dahl et al. (2024) Large Legal Fictions - contra-factual bias
finding: Models often accept a wrong legal premise in the question and cannot judge their own certainty without recalibration.
numbers: Contra-factual tasks pooled by model (Figure 8); Llama 2 rarely hallucinated there but this is partly refusal; rates higher at lower courts.
limits: Interpretation of Llama 2 result is mixed.
agent_relevance: If a case-based prompt carries a wrong precedent, the model tends to accept it. Verify retrieved premises.

source: Zheng et al. (2021) When Does Pretraining Help? CaseHOLD
finding: CaseHOLD asks the model to pick the correct holding of a cited case from five options (53,000+ items). A precedent-understanding test.
numbers: BiLSTM F1 about 0.4; BERT F1 about 0.6; Legal-BERT pretrained on 3.5M US decisions gives +7.2% F1 (12% relative over BERT). Gain larger the more a task resembles the pretraining corpus.
limits: Pre-LLM; multiple choice, not open argument.
agent_relevance: A measurable benchmark for whether a model knows what a precedent stands for. Domain training helps only when tasks are close to the source domain.

source: Guha et al. (2023) LegalBench: collaboratively built benchmark of legal reasoning
finding: Tasks over six reasoning types (issue-spotting, rule-recall, rule-application, rule-conclusion, interpretation, rhetorical-understanding). Rule application needed manual grading of explanations by law-trained reviewers.
numbers: 20 LLMs from 2B to commercial scale; large variation in task difficulty; 119 interpretation tasks, 16 issue-spotting, 16 rule-application, 5 rule-recall.
limits: Per-model table not read; no explicit case-analogy category.
agent_relevance: Legal CBR sits between rule-recall and rule-application; the benchmark has no slot for it.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Precedent-Enhanced Legal Judgment Prediction with LLM and Domain-Model Collaboration (PLJP)
finding: A small domain model proposes candidate labels and retrieves precedents. An LLM then compares the precedents in context and chooses. A retrieve and reuse system.
numbers: Law article accuracy on CJO22: PLJP(CNN) 94.18 vs GPT-3.5-turbo 87.67 vs text-davinci-003 9.13. Ablation row 'w/o p' (read as without precedent) 54.65 accuracy vs 94.18 for full PLJP on the same column.
limits: Chinese criminal data; ablation label read from table order; test set built from cases after Sept 2021.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a precedent step plus LLM comparison beats the LLM alone. Cheap retriever narrows candidates, LLM discriminates.

source: Jiang and Yang (2023) Legal Syllogism Prompting for legal judgment prediction
finding: Zero-shot prompt with major premise (law), minor premise (fact), conclusion beat plain and chain-of-thought prompts on CAIL2018 with GPT-3. Rules-based, not case-based.
numbers: Improvement over baseline and CoT reported; exact table not read.
limits: No exact numbers captured; Chinese charges only.
agent_relevance: The rules-side counterpart to CBR. Legal CBR is rules plus judgement, so combine a syllogism step with case comparison.

source: Nay et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Tax Attorneys
finding: Tested retrieval, few-shot examples and chain of thought for tax questions across OpenAI models. Few-shot examples gave strong gains for GPT-4. Correct legal text lifted accuracy; similarity search gave smaller gains.
numbers: Settings: bypass_retrieval, similarity_search (top 4 passages), gold_truth, lecture_notes, few_shot (3 examples), mega_run. Accuracy rose with each model release; GPT-4 mega_run best but below expert tax lawyers.
limits: Statute based, not precedent; exact percentages in figures not read.
agent_relevance: Retrieval quality (gold versus similarity) mattered. Worked examples help most with strong models.

source: Magesh et al. (2024) - how legal RAG fails
finding: Authors show retrieval fails when wrong passages are retrieved, overruled authority is used, or similar but off-point cases appear.
numbers: Example: Lexis+ AI cited Casey's undue burden standard though overruled.
limits: Qualitative examples, small N.
agent_relevance: Similar-looking cases are not always on point. Check authority and relevance, like Shepardizing.

source: Hatalis et al. (2025) Review of case-based reasoning for LLM agents
finding: Survey fits CBR (retrieve, reuse, revise, retain) to LLM agents and compares to chain-of-thought and standard RAG. Cites Ashley (1988) for CBR in law, CaseGPT and CBR-RAG as legal uses.
numbers: DS-Agent: 100% development-stage success and 99% one-pass deployment with GPT-4 (as reported in the review).
limits: Review, not original experiments; secondary figures; calls for CBR-specific benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Little head-to-head evidence on CBR versus RAG or CoT; we may need our own test.

source: Li et al. (2026) - decomposition of legal case argument
finding: Related work traces HYPO factor representation, CATO hierarchy, CABARET, IBP and VJAP. Arguing with cases needs distinctions, then their significance, then integration.
numbers: Distinction types: emphasizing and downplaying; 253 pairs.
limits: Only trade-secret domain.
agent_relevance: A ready decomposition for a map-an-analogue operator: shared factors, differences, significance of differences, decision.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Towards Supporting Legal Argumentation with NLP: Is More Data Really All You Need?
finding: Review of AI and Law says HYPO (Ashley 1991) and CATO (Aleven 1997) modelled argument moves, while modern legal NLP mostly classifies and lacks justification.
numbers: No numbers; names the gap between statistical prediction and explanation.
limits: Web search quota ran out during this run, so other 2020-2026 LLM studies on HYPO/CATO may exist that were not found.
agent_relevance: The CBR operator should output a justification (cited cases plus distinctions), not just a label.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs - tools versus memory
finding: Online tools matter more than memory on hard long-tail questions.
numbers: HLE: Memento 24.4% PM, second to GPT-5 25.32%; Gemini-2.5-Pro 21.64%, o3-high 20.32%. CoT+RAG baseline 37.7% F1 vs 66.6% with online tools on DeepResearcher.
limits: Effects of tools and memory mixed.
agent_relevance: CBR memory is an add-on to search and checking, not a replacement.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal Question Answering - hybrid case representation
finding: Dual embedding of case question and support text with weights. Cites Rissland and Daniels (1995) hybrid CBR-IR as ancestor.
numbers: Hybrid beat single-embedding in all variants; weights set by grid.
limits: Weights tuned on same data; overfit risk.
agent_relevance: Index cases on more than one facet (facts, issue, outcome).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI) - rules distilled from cases
finding: Insights written by gpt-4 were better than hand-written insights, and adding reflections to insight extraction hurt.
numbers: Hand-crafted insights gave a boost over ReAct but less than LLM insights (Table 3); better base model gives better insights.
limits: Numbers garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Rule abstraction from cases can be automated, but let the stronger model do it.
